what_site_says: HELOC and home equity loan (HELOAN) are both second mortgages, in second position to the first mortgage.

HELOC: revolving line of credit; borrow as needed; interest charged on the amount borrowed; draw period (typically interest-only on the amount used) then repayment period (principal and interest, payments can increase); most HELOCs have variable rates.
HELOAN: lump sum, usually fixed rate, fixed monthly payments over a set period.
Both are secured by the home; failure to repay can lead to foreclosure.
Closing cost categories: appraisal fees, origination fees, title search or recording fees, other administrative costs; ask for a detailed breakdown.
Appraisal: traditional appraisal or automated valuation model (AVM), depending on lender.
Steps: application and documents; credit check; property appraisal; closing costs and closing.
claims_not_to_copy: closings in as little as two weeks
questions_answered: How a HELOC works (draw and repayment)

what_site_says: Cash-out refinance replaces the existing mortgage with a new, larger loan; the difference is received as cash; new rate, term and payment.
Key considerations: interest rate difference, loan-to-value limits, closing costs, risk (home is collateral, higher balance, possibly longer term).
Cash-out refinance vs second mortgage: if you already have a low first-mortgage rate, a refinance of the first mortgage may not be ideal; HELOC or HELOAN are alternatives.
Rate-and-term refinance: change rate and/or term, no cash out.
Loan-type guides: conforming, conventional, FHA, USDA, VA.
claims_not_to_copy: Lower your rate and monthly payment right NOW
could save you thousands of dollars per year

what_site_says: HECM (Home Equity Conversion Mortgage) for homeowners 62 and older; federally insured and regulated by HUD (site wording).
Borrowers must stay current on property taxes and homeowners insurance, keep the home in good condition, and keep it as their primary residence; failing to meet these can make the loan due.
Also responsible for HOA or other required fees.
If you move out for extended periods or convert the home into a rental, the loan could become due.
HUD-approved counseling is required.
Primary residence only; not investment properties or second homes.

Eligible property types: single-family homes; two-to-four unit properties where you occupy one unit; HUD-approved condominiums; newly constructed homes need a Certificate of Occupancy (or equivalent).
Ways to receive proceeds: lump sum, line of credit, monthly payments, combination.

Cost categories: appraisal, origination, closing costs, counseling fee, FHA mortgage insurance premiums; ongoing servicing fees, interest, monthly mortgage insurance premium; most upfront costs can be financed into the loan.
Repayment due when the home is sold or the last surviving borrower or qualified non-borrowing spouse no longer lives there; foreclosure is possible if obligations are not met.
Refers to Reverse Mortgage Specialists at Finance of America Reverse LLC (FAR).

faq_home.q: What is the difference between pre-qualification and pre-approval?
faq_home.a: Pre-qualification is usually an early estimate based on information you provide. A pre-approval involves a deeper review of your credit, income, assets, and debts. Because the information is verified, a pre-approval generally carries more weight with real estate agents and sellers.

faq_home.q: How much do I need for a down payment?
faq_home.a: It depends on the loan program and your financial profile. Some qualified buyers may have low- or no-down-payment options, while a larger down payment may reduce the monthly payment or mortgage-insurance cost. We compare the cash required with the payment and long-term impact.

faq_home.q: What factors affect my mortgage interest rate?
faq_home.a: Credit profile, loan type, property type, occupancy, down payment or equity, loan term, points, and current market conditions can all affect pricing. The lowest advertised rate is not always the lowest total-cost option.

Most borrowers provide identification, income documentation, bank or asset statements, employment history, and information about current debts. Self-employed and alternative-income programs may require different documents. We provide a specific checklist for your loan type.

faq_home.q: Can I qualify with imperfect credit?
faq_home.a: Possibly. Credit requirements vary by loan program, lender, and the rest of your financial profile. Rather than assuming the answer is no, we review the full picture and identify whether an option exists now or whether a focused improvement plan would help.

faq_home.q: How long does the mortgage process take?
faq_home.a: Timelines vary based on the loan, property, appraisal, documentation, and underwriting conditions. A complete application and quick responses help avoid delays. We explain the expected timeline at the beginning and communicate throughout the process.

Refinancing may make sense when the new loan improves your monthly cash flow, interest cost, loan term, payment stability, or access to equity enough to justify the closing costs. We calculate the break-even point and compare it with your expected time in the home.

faq_home.q: What is MIP, and can it be removed?
faq_home.a: Mortgage insurance premium may be required on certain conventional loans when the down payment is below 20%. Cancellation rules depend on the loan, payment history, property value, and applicable guidelines. FHA mortgage insurance follows different rules.
